label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Thursdays on the Tea Trolley**

When Bridget asked me to write this month's piece, she was quite clear about what she wanted: more people for the Thursday tea trolley. So I shall get straight to it. We are a rota of six with only four of us on it. One of our number moved to Sheffield over the summer to be near her grandchildren, and another is recovering from a new knee. We wish them both well, and we would very much like to replace them.

I suspect a good many of you have thought about volunteering here and then talked yourselves out of it. I know the reasons, because I had them too. You imagine it must be terribly upsetting, or that you would need some sort of nursing background, or both. I spent 41 years as a bookkeeper, most of them for a builders' merchant in Dereham. I have no medical knowledge whatsoever. What the tea trolley needs is someone who can push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. The remembering part turns out to be not so different from keeping ledgers straight.

The day therapy unit sees somewhere between 14 and 18 patients on a Thursday afternoon. Some come for the art group, some for the hand massage, and a fair few just for the company. Most of them go home afterwards. It is, I should tell you, a noisy and rather jolly place on a Thursday. There is a lot of laughing, a certain amount of good-natured arguing, and a constant battle over the bourbon biscuits, which always go first. We now hide a packet for the late group. I am not sure that is in the volunteer handbook.

Then there is Mr Hollis, a retired signalman who takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every single week. The details shift a little each time, and the dates move about. I have given up correcting him. It is his story, and it is a good one.

My first week, I tipped an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so hard she had to be handed a tissue, and told me afterwards it was the best afternoon she'd had in a month. I have had worse introductions to a job.

I won't pretend every Thursday is like that. Some weeks are hard. You get to know people, and that is rather the point, so of course there are sad days. When they come, the staff look after us properly. You are never left to manage on your own.

I should also say, since Bridget told me to be honest, that I didn't start this out of any great goodness. I retired, and for about eighteen months I had no regular reason to leave the house most weeks. I drifted. It didn't suit me. I started in March 2022, and Thursdays sorted that out fairly quickly. I get at least as much out of the afternoon as anyone I pour a cup for.

**The practical bits**

- **When:** Thursday afternoons, 1.30 to 4pm, in the day therapy unit.
- **How often:** One Thursday a fortnight. That's all.
- **Training:** Bridget runs an induction of about two hours, and there is a short online food hygiene course, which the hospice pays for.

**Come and have a look**

If you are even half tempted, come to the volunteer open afternoon on **Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits (bourbons, if I have anything to do with it), and there is no obligation whatsoever. You can ask Bridget anything you like, have a look round, and go home and think about it.

If you can't make that, ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she will be glad to have a chat.

And if you already know someone who's retired, at a bit of a loose end, and good at remembering how people take their tea, bring them along too. We need two at the very least, and I'd be delighted to see more.

The kettle will be on.
